strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-motivated gap: contextual bandits whose rewards depend directly on a hidden Markov state (in addition to contexts and actions), with arbitrary state switching rates and continuous rewards. Prior work (Azizzadenesheli et al. 2016; Zhou et al. 2021; Hong et al. 2020; Galozy et al. 2025) either assumes context-free rewards, finite reward spaces, or infrequent latent-state changes, so the setting is a real contribution.

The extension of the reward model beyond the 'belief-linear' model of Nelson et al. (2022) is well argued: Section 3 convincingly shows that the belief-based model (4) reduces to standard linear contextual bandits, whereas the state-dependent model (1) does not, and the tension between Ut-measurability of actions and estimability of beliefs P(h_t=h | F_t) is clearly articulated (Section 3.2).

The staged LinUCB strategy with a carefully constructed filtration U_t, combined with HMM exponential forgetting (Assumption 5.1) and an L2-Markov argument for the difficult S^∆ term, is a coherent and technically careful solution; the proof sketch in Sections 5.3 and Appendices B, D, E is transparent and reproducible in structure.

The treatment of the simplified model (Appendix A) is a clean, self-contained improvement over Nelson et al. (2022): it handles online belief estimation, yields high-probability (not just expected) bounds, removes the reward-gap dependencies, and eliminates the need for the non-degeneracy/coverage assumption on the population design matrix, at the cost of T^{3/4} instead of √T.

The belief-estimation analysis (Appendix C) is a valuable service contribution: it assembles spectral-method guarantees (Hsu et al.; Anandkumar et al.; De Castro et al.; Zhou et al.) into an explicit U_belief(t, δ) error function, adds a nontrivial alignment step to keep hidden-state labels consistent over time, and makes all constants explicit.

The limitations section is honest: the authors clearly flag that the T^{3/4} and T^{7/8} rates are likely suboptimal and identify the L2-Markov inequality (1/√δ_s vs √ln(1/δ_s) dependency) as the source of the polynomial loss, framing these as open questions rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: Numerical experiments are entirely absent: Appendix F literally states 'Numerical simulations will be provided in a version 2 of this article.' For a paper introducing a full algorithm (Box A) with several tuning parameters (λ, ℓ, δ, belief subroutine), the lack of any empirical validation—especially given that rates like T^{7/8} may hide very large constants (the confidence bonus f_t involves many model-dependent constants)—is a significant weakness.

Practical implementability of the confidence bonuses is not addressed. In Theorem 5.2, ε_{t,a} depends on the forgetting constant γ (which is a function of the unknown HMM transition matrix), on C_η, C_θ*, and on the threshold T_{B,M,ν}-related quantities; the paper acknowledges T_{B,M,ν} is 'not necessarily known to the learner' but does not explain how the bonuses can be computed without knowledge of γ and other HMM-dependent constants, nor whether a doubling/adaptive scheme preserves the bound.

The achieved regret rates are weak: T^{3/4} for the simplified model (worse than the √T expected bound of Nelson et al. 2022, though the comparison is complicated by belief estimation and the missing HMM-parameter-estimation cost in their analysis) and T^{7/8} for the main model. No lower bounds are provided, so it remains unclear how much of the gap to √T is fundamental versus an artifact of the L2-Markov technique; the paper acknowledges this but the contribution is thus mostly 'first sublinear bound in a harder model' rather than a near-optimal solution.

The guarantees rely on strong structural assumptions on the HMM (Assumption 4.2: stationary initial distribution, full-rank emission matrix with ε_{ν,min}>0, invertible transition matrix with ε_M>0; Assumption 5.1 forgetting). The known-horizon requirement and knowledge of H further restrict applicability; these restrictions are discussed only sparsely in the main text.

Presentation has noticeable flaws: several incomplete sentences (e.g., Contribution 1 in Section 1 ends with 'to carefully balance' with no continuation), typos ('partiel elements', 'Marhov chain', 'self-completedness', 'an stage'), and a mislabeled assumption in Theorem 5.2 ('Assumption 2.3 (sub-Gaussian noise)' although sub-Gaussian is Assumption 2.2). These do not undermine the mathematics but indicate insufficient polish.

The pseudo-regret benchmark uses beliefs based only on contexts (σ(x_{1:t})), which the authors themselves note is a modeling choice ('somewhat unnatural' when done as in Zhou et al. 2021); Remark 2.4 gestures at an actual-regret extension 'by adapting the proof' but this is not fully carried out, which slightly weakens the claim of intrinsic benchmarking.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine modeling gap: prior work on contextual bandits with HMM latent dynamics (notably Nelson et al., 2022) assumed rewards linear in the belief (posterior over states) rather than directly in the hidden state, and the paper convincingly argues this reduction (Section 3.1) is a substantive simplification rather than a harmless variation.

The paper delivers high-probability regret guarantees where prior work offered only in-expectation bounds, with self-contained, detailed proofs (Appendices A–E), including a careful extension of the elliptical potential lemma to staged updates (Lemma E.6) and a clean treatment of the labeling/alignment issue for spectrally estimated HMM states (Appendix C.2).

The algorithm design is principled: the tension between action measurability and estimability of beliefs is clearly articulated (Section 3.2), and the staged filtration U_t exploiting HMM forgetting is a sensible and well-motivated construction.

The belief-estimation subroutine is treated generically via Assumption 4.1, with a concrete instantiation (spectral method + Bayes updates + alignment) grounding the assumption in known results, making the framework reusable.
The limitations section (Section 6) is honest about the main open questions, including the suboptimality of the T^{7/8} rate stemming from the L^2–Markov argument.
weaknesses: The submission is incomplete. Appendix F, the only place where empirical validation would appear, is literally a one-line placeholder: 'Numerical simulations will be provided in a version 2 of this article.' For a method paper whose guarantees involve large constants (T_B,M,ν with an opaque closed form, λ = T^{3/4}, ℓ = ⌈T^{3/4}⌉), the absence of any experiment leaves the practicality of the approach completely unaddressed and suggests the manuscript was not ready for submission.

The writing shows unfinished quality beyond the missing experiments: the contribution summary in Section 1 ends mid-sentence ('...proceeding in stages to carefully balance'), and there are typos such as 'partiel elements', duplicated words ('may be be estimated'), and 'a in a more direct and more efficient way'. In Theorem 5.2, Assumption 2.3 is mislabeled as '(sub-Gaussian noise)' when the sub-Gaussian condition is Assumption 2.2.

The main regret rate T^{7/8} is weak and no lower bound is provided. The gap to the T^{3/4} rate of the simplified model, or even to the √T rate achievable when beliefs are known, is unresolved and attributed to the L^2–Markov technique, which introduces 1/√δ dependencies. The paper itself concedes this (Section 6), so the headline result may be far from tight; there is no evidence the T^{1/8} price is fundamental.

The theoretical contribution is largely incremental relative to Nelson et al. (2022): the difficult term S^Δ is explicitly handled by mimicking 'the key technical contribution by Nelson et al. (2022)' (Appendix E.1.1), and the simplified-model analysis (Appendix A) is a fairly direct LinUCB adaptation. The belief estimation machinery is borrowed wholesale from Anandkumar et al., Azizzadenesheli et al., Zhou et al., and De Castro et al., with the paper itself stating 'We provide no methodological development on the estimation of beliefs'.

The assumptions are restrictive relative to the claimed generality: the concrete belief-estimation guarantee (Lemma 4.3) requires finite contexts, a full-rank emission matrix, a strictly positive transition matrix, and a stationary initial distribution; the continuous-context case (Example 2) is deferred to references without a stated guarantee. Additionally, the main theorem requires a known horizon T with T-dependent parameters (λ, ℓ), and confidence bonuses depend on the unknown threshold T_B,M,ν whose interaction with the guarantee deserves more discussion.

The pseudo-regret benchmark (2) uses beliefs based only on contexts (F^bnk_t = σ(x_{1:t})), which is stronger than the natural oracle; Remark 2.4 claims the actual-regret version follows 'by adapting the proof' but this is asserted rather than proven. The argument that this benchmark choice is 'more intrinsic' (Section 2.2) is thin.

No comparison, even qualitative, is given against the change-point / non-stationary latent bandit line (Hong et al., 2020; Galozy et al., 2025) in terms of actual regret rates under comparable assumptions; the positioning relies on the argument that those works degrade to linear regret under linear-rate switching, but the HMM forgetting assumptions here also constrain the environment class.

strengths: The paper identifies and rigorously formalizes a genuine gap in the literature: Nelson et al. (2022) study a simplified reward model where rewards are linear in the posterior beliefs rather than in the hidden states themselves, and the authors clearly explain (Sections 3.1-3.2, Appendix A) why the belief-based model reduces to linear contextual bandits while the state-dependent model (1) does not.

The T^{7/8} high-probability regret bound for the general state-dependent model appears to be the first sublinear guarantee for this setting (rewards jointly dependent on states, contexts, and actions, with arbitrarily frequent latent switches and continuous rewards), where prior work either assumed infrequent changes, context-free rewards, finite reward spaces, or benchmarks knowing realized states.

The analysis is technically careful and self-contained: the construction of the intermediate filtration U_t balancing action measurability with belief estimability, the staged L2-Markov argument extending Nelson et al.'s technique (Appendices B and E), the staged elliptic potential lemma (Lemma E.6), and the alignment step ensuring consistent hidden-state labeling (Appendix C.2) are all worked out in detail with closed-form constants.

The results are stronger in several relevant dimensions than prior guarantees: high probability rather than in expectation, reward-model-free (gap-free) dependence, no coverage/nondegeneracy assumption on the population design matrix, and a milder noise assumption (bounded conditional second moments, Assumption 2.3) for the main theorem.

The limitations and open questions section is honest and specific, correctly flagging that the T^{7/8} and T^{3/4} rates may not be optimal and identifying the 1/sqrt(delta) dependency from the Markov argument as the likely culprit.
weaknesses: There are no numerical simulations whatsoever; Appendix F states only that 'Numerical simulations will be provided in a version 2 of this article.' This is a significant deficiency for a main-track submission, especially since Section C.4 even refers to 'our numerical experiments' (suggesting results exist but were not included), and the practical behavior of the staged algorithm with spectral belief estimation and horizon-dependent parameters (lambda = T^{3/4}) is entirely unvalidated.

The regret rates are weak and no lower bounds are provided: T^{7/8} for the general model and T^{3/4} for the simplified model, the latter being strictly worse than the sqrt(T) expected bound of Nelson et al. (2022) (though the extra factor is attributed to belief estimation and to removing a coverage assumption). Without lower bounds, it is unclear how much of the gap is fundamental versus an artifact of the analysis, and the paper admits the L2-Markov technique likely costs a polynomial factor.

The contribution is best characterized as a careful extension and correction of a single specific prior work (Nelson et al., 2022); the significance rests on the premise that the belief-based reward model is an 'important simplification,' which, while argued convincingly, makes the contribution somewhat specialized.

Strong structural assumptions are needed for the belief estimation subroutine: finite context set with full-rank emission matrix, uniformly positive minimal emission/transition entries, invertible transition matrix, and stationary initialization (Assumption 4.2). The number of hidden states H must be known, and the threshold T_{B,M,nu} is unknown to the learner yet enters the regret bound; the horizon T must also be known to set lambda and the stage length.

Presentation inconsistencies and typos undermine polish: Assumption 2.3 is mislabeled '(sub-Gaussian noise)' in the statements of Theorems 5.2 and E.1 (it is the bounded-second-moment assumption; 2.2 is the sub-Gaussian one), a truncated sentence in Section 1 ('...carefully balance'), and several typos ('partiel elements', 'an stage', 'Marhov chain', 'self-completedness', the truncated Nelson et al. sentence in Section 5.1).

No code or reproducibility material is provided, and the pseudo-regret benchmark based on beliefs conditioned only on contexts (F^{bnk}_t = sigma(x_{1:t})) is defensible but contestable; Remark 2.4's claim that actual regret could be handled is deferred rather than proven.
